Plain Speech
playn speech
noun phrase (honest, simple speech)
From “plain” (Latin planus, flat, clear) and “speech”; the honest, simple, truthful speech the Lord commands — yea meaning yea, and nay meaning nay.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

Plain speech is the honest, simple, truthful speech the Lord commands of His people: “Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.” James repeats it: “Let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.” The teaching forbids the manipulative oath-taking, the evasive equivocation, and the doubled and slippery word by which men deceive while keeping the letter of truth; the disciple's bare word is to be as binding as another man's oath, because he speaks in the presence of God who hates lying lips and delights in them that deal truly. Paul appeals to the same standard: “as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay”—not double, not shifting. The dictionary marks plain speech against the whole craft of deceitful communication: the flattery that says what it does not mean, the spin that technically avoids a lie while intending one, the broken promise dressed in fine words, and the mental reservation that betrays trust. It is not bluntness for its own sake, nor the rudeness that wounds under cover of “just being honest”; plain speech is truthful speech spoken in love, simple and reliable. The man of plain speech can be trusted on his word alone, for he reckons that he answers to God for every idle word, and that whatsoever exceeds the simple truth cometh of evil.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The honest, simple, truthful speech the Lord commands — yea meaning yea, nay meaning nay (Matthew 5:37; James 5:12); the bare word as binding as an oath, against equivocation, spin, and the deceitful doubled word.

PLAIN SPEECH, noun phrase. Honest, simple, truthful speech.

“Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay” (Matthew 5:37).

“Let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay” (James 5:12).

The disciple's bare word is as binding as an oath, spoken before God.

Against equivocation, spin, flattery, and the deceitful doubled word.

📖 Key Scripture

Mt 5:37 — "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil."

Jas 5:12 — "But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation."

Pr 12:22 — "Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight."

2 Co 1:18 — "But as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The age corrupts plain speech with spin, equivocation, and the technically-true lie; the opposite error is the rudeness that wounds under cover of “just being honest.”

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the binding truthfulness of the simple word. The age has perfected the craft of saying what is technically true while intending to deceive—spin, equivocation, the doubled and slippery word, the promise worded to be broken, the flattery that means nothing. The Lord forbids it all: let your yea be yea. The disciple's bare word is to be as reliable as another man's sworn oath, for he speaks before the God who hates lying lips and delights in them that deal truly; whatsoever exceeds the simple truth cometh of evil.

The opposite corruption hides cruelty behind candor—the rudeness that wounds and excuses itself with “I'm just being honest.” Plain speech is not bluntness for its own sake nor a license to bludgeon. It is truthful speech spoken in love, simple and trustworthy. The dictionary holds both edges: against the deceiver, the word must be true and reliable; against the brawler, the true word must be seasoned with grace. The man of plain speech can be trusted on his word alone, and he speaks that truth not to wound but to edify, knowing he answers to God for every word.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Latin planus (flat, clear) and the Lord's command of the simple “yea” and “nay”; truthful speech that needs no oath to be believed.

expand to see more

Planus, Latin, flat, level, clear—the root of “plain.”

“Yea, yea; Nay, nay” (Greek nai nai, ou ou), the Lord's standard of speech.

The bare word made as binding as an oath (Matthew 5:33-37).

Emeth, Hebrew, truth, the dealing-truly that is the LORD's delight (Proverbs 12:22).

Against the doubled, shifting word—“yea and nay” (2 Corinthians 1:18).

Usage

"The elder kept plain speech, his bare word as good as another man's bond."

"The pastor rebuked the spin that tells a technical truth to leave a false impression."

"She spoke the truth in love, neither deceiving with smooth words nor wounding under cover of honesty."
